consensus_summary: The blind consensus identifies 'the truth' primarily as Jesus Christ himself, the personal embodiment of divine revelation (John 14:6), with closely allied referents: God's word/the gospel message, the Spirit of truth, sound doctrine, God's covenant faithfulness, and moral integrity. The Christological-personal identification is the settled center across all four responses.
book_summary: The book identifies 'the truth' as God's law — the standard. It explicitly flags the common teaching (Christ Himself, and God's word/gospel that sets free) as the view it departs from, citing Ps 119:142 ('thy law is the truth') and 2 John 4.
consensus_core_identification: Christ himself as the personal embodiment of divine truth, extended to God's word and the gospel that reveals him.
book_core_identification: God's law as the standard — 'the truth' is the divine law, not the person of Christ or the gospel message.
boundary_disagreement: The book excludes the consensus's central cases — Christ in person (John 14:6) and the gospel message (Eph 1:13; Col 1:5) — while retaining only the Old Testament word/law strand (Ps 119:142) that the consensus treats as a secondary alternative or background. It effectively reclassifies Johannine 'truth that sets free' from gospel to law.
material_contradiction: The consensus core is a person (Christ) and the liberating gospel; the book's core is the law as standard. The book's own common-view note contrasts its identification against 'Christ Himself, and God's word — the gospel that sets free,' signaling deliberate replacement rather than refinement. In classical theology law and gospel are distinct categories, so identifying 'the truth' as the law-standard rather than the person of Christ or the gospel cannot both be the same core identification in the same sense.
rationale: Both the primary meanings across all four blind responses and their notes converge on a Christological-personal center for 'the truth,' with God's word/gospel as its immediate extension. The book replaces that center with 'God's law — the standard.' While 'law as truth' appears within the consensus (Ps 119:142 is cited by Responses A, C, and D under the word-of-God alternative), it is there subordinate background to the Christological reading, never the core. Because the book elevates the law-standard to the sole identification and explicitly sets it against the commonly taught Christ/gospel reading, this is replacement of the central referent, not mere narrowing of an intact category — hence DIVERGENT with partial extensional overlap (the Psalm 119 word/law cases are retained; the Christ-person and gospel cases are reclassified out).
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED rather than DIVERGENT: 'God's law' is a subset of 'God's word,' which the consensus already lists as a dominant referent for truth (John 17:17; Ps 119:142, 160), so the book might be seen as merely narrowing an accepted category rather than replacing the Christological core. Additionally, Ps 119:142 verbatim states 'thy law is the truth,' giving the book direct textual footing within consensus proof texts.
